item.title: NASA’s Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Before astronauts return to the lunar surface, NASA will first conduct one of the most ambitious and complex test missions in the agency’s history.

Launching in 2027, Artemis III will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano aboard the Orion spacecraft into low Earth orbit to perform a series of demonstrations with test versions, or test articles, of human landing systems being developed by industry partners Blue Origin and SpaceX. During the planned 14-day mission, crews and flight controllers will practice the rendezvous, docking, habitation, and operational procedures that will be essential when Artemis astronauts begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole in 2028. The mission is designed to reduce risk, validate hardware, and gain operational experience before NASA attempts a crewed lunar landing.

“Every piece of this mission in Earth orbit is designed to reduce risk before we put astronauts back on the Moon,” said Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager. “We’re launching three spacecraft on three different rockets and testing how they operate together — something NASA has never attempted. Every lesson we learn here gets us closer to landing on the Moon in 2028.”

First stop: Blue Origin’s lunar lander test article 

Earlier Artemis missions used only NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft. Artemis III will involve three separate spacecraft launched on three different heavy-lift rockets within a relatively short period of time.

The mission begins with Blue Origin launching a test version of its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander into a circular low Earth orbit approximately 273 miles (237 nautical miles) above Earth. The spacecraft can remain on orbit for up to 30 days providing schedule flexibility. Artemis III is designed as a tightly choreographed campaign, with NASA planning to launch Orion on top of SLS from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida only days after the Blue Moon test article launch and confirmation the vehicle is healthy and ready for joint operations.

Following launch, Orion will initially enter an elliptical Earth orbit of 18 x 1122 miles (16 x 975 nautical miles). It will use its service module to perform a series of maneuvers to transition to a circular orbit at about 345 miles (300 nautical miles) for thermal stabilization before then gradually setting up its rendezvous with the waiting Blue Moon lander test article. Because each spacecraft operates in slightly different orbital regimes optimized for its mission requirements, Artemis III requires a carefully choreographed sequence of orbital maneuvers and rendezvous operations throughout the flight.

During the first two days of flight, the crew will check out Orion’s systems, prepare for proximity operations, and gradually position themselves for the mission’s first major objective: rendezvous and docking with the Blue Moon test vehicle.

The operation represents NASA’s first opportunity to evaluate how Orion and a commercial lunar lander work together in space. Engineers will assess how software aboard both spacecraft, guidance systems, communications systems, and operational procedures perform in real-world conditions, while flight controllers gain experience coordinating activities across multiple teams and organizations.

Once docked, astronauts will spend approximately two days conducting evaluations aboard the Blue Moon test article. Crew members will open the hatch and enter the spacecraft, allowing them to assess the cabin environment, controls, and life-support systems firsthand. Teams will verify the spacecraft’s ability to maintain the proper atmosphere and pressure.

The Blue Moon test article incorporates many of the avionics, software, flight-control systems, crew-cabin technologies, and life-support functions planned for future lunar missions. Testing those systems in orbit will provide the first opportunity to evaluate how many of the lander’s flight systems perform in space as an integrated vehicle.

By the time Orion undocks, NASA will have completed its first evaluation of a commercial lunar lander with crew, gathering data on spacecraft systems, crew operations, and spacecraft interoperability not possible on the ground.

Starship docking demonstration  

After completing operations with Blue Origin’s lander, Orion will undock and reposition to support the next phase of the mission: a second rendezvous operation.

SpaceX will launch a Starship Version 3 test article from Florida. Because Starship is designed for a much shorter on-orbit lifetime than Blue Origin’s lander, launch occurs later in the mission, allowing NASA to efficiently sequence the two docking demonstrations. Starship will enter a lower orbit at 206 nautical miles, optimized for communications coverage, and will carry an added docking system mounted at the forward end.

Orion will rendezvous and dock with the spacecraft during a test expected to last up to two hours. Crew will not enter Starship during this test. The demonstration is focused on validating how Orion and Starship interact as a docked system in space. NASA and SpaceX plan to evaluate spacecraft controllability, communications, integrated software performance, and the dynamics associated with docking and undocking operations.

The docking itself also presents a unique test, using different docking geometries. Orion will connect to a port beside Blue Moon’s crew cabin, then later align its forward docking system with the one at Starship’s nose. Testing both approaches during a single mission gives NASA an opportunity to assess different operational concepts while gathering valuable engineering data.

Together, the two docking campaigns will demonstrate how Orion interfaces with two very different commercial lander architectures during a single mission.

Testing Orion for future exploration 

Even after docking activities are complete, Artemis III will continue generating data that supports future missions.

Once the Starship demonstration is complete, Orion and its crew will have up to five additional days available in orbit before beginning preparations for the journey home. NASA plans to use this time to complete a variety of test objectives that support future Artemis missions, including additional evaluations of the Orion Crew Survival System suits, docking sensor tests, acoustic and thermal measurements, human-factors assessments, and a range of science and technology demonstrations.

Several investigations led by NASA will build on studies conducted during Artemis II, collecting additional data that will help inform future deep-space missions. The crew also will conduct a proof-of-concept study examining how astronauts could perform health-related assessments when they are unable to communicate directly with mission control, an important capability for future lunar surface expeditions and other missions farther from Earth.

NASA also plans to fly a cellular biology experiment during the mission while researchers use the flight to test concepts for returning lunar samples to Earth. Teams will evaluate how future samples could be transported, received, and moved into curation facilities after landing, while also conducting assessments of Orion’s environment to better understand potential contamination considerations for future lunar missions.

The mission also will include Earth and solar observations that help astronauts continue developing critical observation skills while taking advantage of the spacecraft’s unique orbital vantage point. Plant seeds will fly aboard Orion as well, providing opportunities for scientific study and educational engagement following the mission.

Mission planners have also built flexibility into the flight timeline, providing additional opportunities to complete test objectives depending on how operations unfold in real time.

When ready, Orion will begin phasing for return, and the crew will configure the cabin for reentry and splashdown, which will occur in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California. Orion and its crew will be recovered by NASA personnel and the United States Navy.

Practicing for Moon missions 

Every activity performed during Artemis III supports a larger goal: reducing risk before astronauts return to the lunar surface.

The mission will provide NASA with experience operating alongside multiple commercial partners while managing complex rendezvous and docking operations involving three different spacecraft. Engineers will gain insight into spacecraft interoperability, mission-control coordination, communications architecture, crew operations, and hardware performance.

By the time Artemis III concludes with Orion’s splashdown on Earth, NASA will have demonstrated technologies and operational concepts that future lunar crews will rely on as they travel to and from the Moon.

Most importantly, Artemis III will provide the operational experience needed to transform plans for future lunar landings into proven flight procedures. The lessons learned throughout the mission will help refine future exploration plans, strengthen partnerships with industry, and ensure astronauts are prepared for humanity’s next giant leap at the Moon.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

item.title: NASA Outlines the Details of Artemis III and IV Missions - Payload Space
item.description:
NASA still wants to return US astronauts to the Moon in 2028. Today, officials shared a progress update on their efforts, as well as the finer details of the mission plans for Artemis III and IV, targeting flights in 2027 and 2028, respectively.

Long story short: NASA remains confident it can meet the timeline for both missions.

The agenda: For Artemis III, NASA is planning to fly a 14- to 17-day mission in LEO, testing three launch vehicles, one lunar lander, and the Orion crew capsule:

  • The mission will begin with an uncrewed launch of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, carrying the company’s Blue Moon test lander.
  • NASA’s SLS rocket will launch the Artemis III crew and the Orion spacecraft to orbit “as soon as we can thereafter,” according to NASA Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons.
  • On Day 3, or once both spacecraft are in orbit, Orion and the Blue Moon test lander will attempt to rendezvous and dock.
  • On Days 4 and 5, the crew will enter Blue Moon to validate the lander’s subsystems—including tests of environmental controls, life-support systems, and emergency scenarios.
  • On Day 6, SpaceX’s Starship will launch to orbit.
  • On Day 8, Starship will attempt to rendezvous and dock with the crewed Orion vehicle. The Artemis III crew won’t transfer from Orion to Starship during this two-hour test, but officials didn’t share why.
  • Following the Starship docking demo, the Artemis III crew will use the remaining days of the mission to complete additional tests on Orion, including tests of the new survival suit.

Above and beyond: For Artemis IV, NASA officials laid out two different mission plans—one using SpaceX’s Starship launcher and human landing system (HLS), and the other using Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket and Mark 2 lander.

While officials didn’t confirm which company would be selected for the historic lunar landing attempt, they said that both companies are making progress, and either or both could be ready in time for NASA’s end-of-2028 goal.

There’s still a long road ahead for both companies, as Blue Origin has yet to return New Glenn to flight following its on-the-pad explosion in May, and SpaceX just notched its first uncrewed orbital flight with Starship in September.

Even still, officials remained confident that both companies will have more than enough launches under their belt before the Artemis IV planning team gets antsy.

“You will have multiple launches of Starship before we go conduct Artemis III, and you will have multiple launches of the Blue Origin New Glenn vehicle from the rebuilt pad before we go launch Artemis III, and so that’s going to give us a lot of confidence,” Parsons said.

Officials also confirmed that SpaceX will attempt to demonstrate its ability to transfer propulsion in orbit in early 2027, a key capability in the company’s plans to get its HLS to the lunar surface.

Zoom out: As he did at Payload’s Off World event last month, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman spent the bulk of his time at the lectern explaining why NASA wants to reach the Moon in two years: Once again, it’s all about beating China. 

Earlier this year, Isaacman predicted China would send a crewed mission around the moon in 2027, and that NASA ‘dodged a bullet’ when the uncrewed Chang’e-6 lander targeting the Moon’s south pole (near water resources both the China and US want) was delayed from this year. As such, he maintained the US should not relax its pace to reach the Moon.

“Here we are today, very much in a new space race, and despite decades of accumulated knowledge and extraordinary advancements in technology, this race will be much closer than it ever needed to be,” Isaacman said at the Friday update. “We will never launch until we are ready, but we will not accept that great achievements simply require more time and more money, nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass [to] our overseas competitors.”

Isaacman was upfront about the agency’s efforts to keep to its self-imposed timeline, and recently told the NASA workforce that Artemis III is, on paper, about 90 days behind schedule—but not for a lack of effort.

Throughout the press conference, NASA officials gave countless examples of how the agency is working with vendors to accelerate supply chains, stretch hardware capabilities to do more (specifically, updates to create a “stretch” Vulcan rocket for Artemis III), and shrink requirements (i.e. on the Axiom spacesuit) to meet tighter deadlines for Artemis IV.

“Every time we run into a supplier issue, a priority issue across the industry, Administrator Isaacman [and Associate Administrator] Amit [Kshatriya] are immediately on the phone. They’re immediately putting pressure. We’re immediately going out and helping to make things happen,” Parsons said.

NASA Shares Artemis Acceleration Plans for Moon Missions

In an update Friday, Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders provided the agency’s path forward to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028. The briefing included details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and information about acceleration efforts to ensure the success of Artemis IV, the first Artemis mission on the lunar surface.

item.title: When will SpaceX and Blue Origin fly to the moon? NASA reveals lunar lander timelines (and an Artemis III update) - Space
item.description:
NASA has revealed new details about its plans to return astronauts to the surface of the moon, outlining a series of upcoming milestones for SpaceX and Blue Origin as both companies race to ready their lunar landers for the agency's Artemis program.

During an Oct. 5 presentation at the Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye, Steve Creech, acting manager of NASA's Human Landing System (HLS) Program, laid out development timelines for both spacecraft, with key demonstrations planned through early 2028 that include orbital refueling and uncrewed lunar landing tests to qualify the vehicles to fly astronauts to the surface of the moon.

A more pressing deadline, however, is NASA's Artemis III mission, which is targeted for the third quarter (Q3) of 2027. Artemis III will launch four astronauts aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft to low Earth orbit (LEO), where they will rendezvous and dock with test versions of both companies' landers for interoperability checkouts. Those demonstrations will help inform NASA's determination about which lander the agency will choose to carry astronauts to the moon's surface on Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.

SpaceX and Blue Origin were both awarded NASA contracts to develop HLS vehicles — Starship and Blue Moon, respectively — and have spent the past several years refining their respective lunar lander designs and dealing with various delays along the way. In the face of those delays, and in an effort to better structure its mission progression for success, NASA overhauled its Artemis program architecture in February to maintain its goal of landing astronauts on the moon by the end of 2028 and establish a more regular cadence of uncrewed landings in the meantime.

As part of that shakeup, Artemis III, previously the program's first crewed lunar landing mission, was moved up a year and repurposed for the lunar lander vehicle tests the agency is preparing to fly to LEO next year. The program's first moon landing remains scheduled for 2028, but was shifted to the manifest for Artemis IV.

Between now and then, both SpaceX and Blue Origin have more than a dozen test demonstrations and vehicle milestones to achieve, including success during Artemis III and flights afterward. This will all lead up to a key decision NASA must make: Which vehicle will carry out the first crewed landing on the surface of the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972?

Starship reached for the first time on its most recent test flight, which occurred on Sept. 28 from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. NASA lists several other important goals for the vehicle to achieve in 2026, including (in the order listed during the IAC presentation) the first return and catch of the rocket's upgraded Version 3 (V3) booster at its launch pad; the first-ever return and catch of a Ship upper stage; the first Starship launch from one of SpaceX's launch pads still under construction on Florida's Space Coast; and, possibly, the first V3 booster reflight.

NASA also expects SpaceX to complete the initial build of the crew cabin for its lunar lander Starship variant. SpaceX released renders of Starship's interior last year, as well as images of the test elevator astronauts are using to train for Starship egress on the lunar surface, but little else has been made public about the progress the company has made on the cabin's design.

Should the cabin's initial build wrap up by the end of the year, as NASA's presentation suggested, SpaceX will use Q1 2027 to complete integration of the systems that Starship will need to communicate with Orion during Artemis III, and deliver a cabin simulator for astronauts to train on leading up to the mission. SpaceX plans to continue Starship test flights through Q2 of next year, complete a landing leg demonstration and begin crew cabin airlock tests.

For Artemis III, SpaceX plans to fly one of its existing V3 Starship upper stages, with some slight modifications. Starship and Orion will dock as part of Artemis III but the SpaceX vehicle won't be equipped with a crew cabin for the mission's astronauts to enter. Between the end of this year and the beginning of the next, SpaceX is expected to complete the addition of a docking system and nosecone cover to the Artemis III Starship vehicle, which, NASA documents suggest, has already completed its mechanical fit checks.

Other notches on SpaceX's checklist leading up to Artemis III include the first propellant transfer demonstration with Starship in orbit. As the first-ever launch vehicle and spacecraft designed for full reusability, Starship's fuel constraints require that its tanks be topped off in order to fly beyond LEO. For a moon landing mission, this could mean up to a dozen launches of SpaceX's Starship "tanker" spacecraft to an orbiting fuel depot, which the moon-bound Starship will visit. To pull that off, though, SpaceX has to show it can successfully transfer those cryogenic fuels on orbit, and also store them effectively enough to prevent too much boil-off.

Starship won't require any refueling flights to complete its objectives for Artemis III, but SpaceX is expected to launch its first Starship tanker vehicle within a few months of that mission as it gears up for the Artemis IV moon landing mission. To that end, a launch of an uncrewed Starship lunar lander variant is targeted sometime toward the end of Q3/beginning of Q4, with an uncrewed lunar landing mission carried out before the end of 2027.

Blue Origin, meanwhile, has its own set of milestones to meet as it develops its Blue Moon Mark 2 (MK2) lander — a 52-foot-tall (16 meters) spacecraft powered by three BE-7 engines. Unlike the bare-bones V3 Starship that SpaceX will launch on Artemis III, Blue Origin plans to fly a completed test vehicle, incorporating the crew cabin, partial life-support, flight software and other systems needed to allow astronauts to enter the lander from Orion during their time docked in LEO. Astronauts will be able to enter Blue Moon from Orion to get a feel for the lander in zero-g and test some of its systems.

NASA's timeline shows the company working to complete a series of manufacturing and testing milestones in the last few months of 2026, including continued BE-7 testing and qualification of Blue Moon's BT-7 maneuvering thrusters. The company also faces its Artemis III interim design review and a critical design review for an upcoming landing demonstration mission in 2028.

Blue Origin is also working to restore its pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station's Launch Complex-36 (LC-36) to operation and return its New Glenn rocket to flight, following an explosion of the rocket in May that caused extensive damage to the facility. NASA's presentation places that milestone in Q4 2026, a timeline the company has also been very vocal about maintaining. A recent Reuters report, however, suggests that may not happen until early 2027.

By early 2027, the company expects to complete the spacecraft's communications systems and finalize its flight software, with assembly, integration and testing continuing into Q2. Q1 2027 is also when Blue Origin's Blue Moon MK1 lander (a smaller, uncrewed version of its MK2 successor) will launch to the lunar surface as a part of NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program of robotic moon missions.

During Q2 2027, as the Artemis III mission approaches, Blue Origin is expected to complete integration of its test lander with New Glenn and conclude qualification of its BE-7 engine. Throughout next year, the company plans to continue construction and refurbishments at its launch facilities and hopes to have a new launch pad ready to support the upgraded, more powerful New Glenn 9x4 rocket l by the end of Q3. The first flight of that rocket variant is scheduled for Q4 2027, alongside a second MK1 lunar mission and the launch of an uncrewed MK2 demonstration lander.

That spacecraft is expected to attempt its own uncrewed lunar landing in Q1 2028, around the same time Blue Origin has scheduled a third MK1 flight. Like SpaceX, Blue Origin will need to demonstrate that its lander can safely reach the moon's surface,operate there and return to lunar orbit before NASA clears it to carry astronauts on a future Artemis mission.

NASA's overall timeline remains the same as it has been since the February revamp, with Artemis III expected to launch in mid-2027, followed by a crewed lunar landing on Artemis IV in 2028, and possibly another on Artemis V that same year. There may be changes on the horizon, though. NASA will host a press conference on Friday (Oct. 23) with Administrator Jared Isaacman and Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya, as well as Artemis program director Jeremy Parsons. During the event, which you'll be able to watch here at Space.com, they will discuss the status of the upcoming moon missions and an "Artemis acceleration."

SpaceX and Blue Origin still face tight schedules to complete their respective uncrewed landing demonstrations before Artemis IV. With SpaceX targeting Q4 2027 and Blue Origin Q1 2028, both are pushing the margins against NASA's hopes to return astronauts to the lunar surface that same year. Which company ultimately gets the green light for that first landing mission will depend on the progress each makes between now and then, and whether their landers can demonstrate the readiness that NASA requires to safely carry astronauts to the surface of the moon and back again.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and space exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions from the Space Coast, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon and more. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

item.title: Watch NASA's update on accelerating Artemis moon plans today - Space
item.description:
NASA will provide an update about its Artemis moon plans on Friday (Oct. 23), and you can watch it live.

The news will come during a press conference at the agency's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, which starts Friday at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT). You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA.

"The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and how plans to return American astronauts to the moon by 2028 are progressing," NASA officials said in an Oct. 14 media advisory.

Three agency officials will participate in Friday's "Artemis Acceleration" event. They are:

  • NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman
  • NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya
  • Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis programmanager

NASA is currently gearing up for Artemis III, which is targeted for mid-2027. The mission will test rendezvous and docking technologies between NASA's Orion capsule and one or both of the private spacecraft that NASA picked to be the Artemis program's crewed lunar landers: SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

After that will come Artemis IV, which will land astronauts near the lunar south pole in early 2028, if all goes to plan. That will be the first crewed moon touchdown since Apollo 17 way back in 1972.

It's unclear which lunar lander will fly on Artemis IV; that depends on how the development of each one progresses and what happens on Artemis III.

And there will be other landings after Artemis IV. NASA plans to establish a moon base via Artemis, and doing so will require a variety of missions, both robotic and crewed.

The agency feels some urgency in this quest, for China has similar goals. It's important that the U.S. wins this new space race, military and political officials have said, so that the nation can establish the norms of responsible behavior on Earth's nearest neighbor.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. item.title: NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update

Progress on NASA’s Artemis III’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket continues at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where teams have completed the integration of the final solid rocket booster motor segments onto the mobile launcher for the “short stack” configuration that will be used during a tanking test. Teams also completed installation of all four RS-25 engines on the SLS core stage.

Teams now will install the systems tunnel that runs the length of the core stage and is used to route pyrotechnic cabling, a system of wiring that allows the single-use, quick disconnect for controlled movements during liftoff, on the massive stage. In the coming weeks, the stage will be integrated with the solid rocket boosters, completing the rocket’s “short stack” configuration.

NASA will roll the short stack SLS rocket from the spaceport’s Vehicle Assembly Building to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test in the coming months, where the Artemis launch team will practice procedures and timelines for loading propellant. While at the pad, the Artemis III crew, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, also will conduct a launch day rehearsal and emergency exit walkdown. This will include suiting up in astronaut crew quarters, driving to the launch pad, ascending the mobile launcher, and then walking through the exit route they would take in the unlikely event of an emergency during launch countdown.

Additional hardware updates

At Launch Pad 39B, teams continue the refurbishment of the flame deflector, which saw minimal damage after the Artemis II launch. The bricks on the flame trench itself were not affected by the launch due to ground support improvements informed by lessons learned after Artemis I in 2022.

Teams are continuing to work through testing on the Orion spacecraft. Recently, engineers with ESA and Airbus inspected the solar array wings, which deliver power to the service module that provides propulsion, thermal control, and electrical power to the spacecraft, as well as air and water for the crew.

At NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the forward and aft rings were welded on the Artemis III spacer, completing the primary structure. The spacer will serve to represent upper stage dimensions during the mission. The dimensional checks are underway.

Engineers also are converting two existing structural test articles, the Orion stage adapter and launch vehicle stage adapter, into flight-ready hardware. Exterior painting on the Orion stage adapter was recently completed at NASA Marshall, with cables and brackets to be installed soon. The launch vehicle stage adapter has undergone detailed inspection and preparation, with corrosion removal nearly complete, and nondestructive evaluation will begin this fall. Following that evaluation, technicians will apply conversion coating to the interior, prime and paint the exterior, and spray the cone-shaped adapter with thermal protection spray foam.

The spacer and both adapters remain on track to ship to Kennedy early next year.

Crew training continues

The Artemis III crew has continued a variety of training activities to prepare for their mission. Recently, they completed lessons on the flywheel exercise device, practicing hardware setup, anticipated exercises, and equipment disassembly. This compact device, about the size of an extra-large shoe box, uses pulleys and a torque limiter to mimic a rowing machine, allowing aerobic, resistive, and rowing exercises with straps attached to either a bar or harness.

Nutrition also is a key focus. At NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory in Houston, crew members sampled nearly 200 items on the menu to select their favorites for the mission, ensuring their health and performance are supported throughout.

The crew concluded helicopter underwater egress training, practicing escape from a submerged, upside-down mock helicopter cabin in a controlled pool environment to prepare for potential off-nominal water crash-landings.

Last week, members of the Artemis III crew traveled to San Diego to participate in recovery training with NASA and military partners, practicing water lifts by U.S. Navy helicopters.

They completed several suited training activities in the Orion Crew Survival System Suits this week, preparing for post-insertion, deorbit procedures, and emergency responses. These activities included communication system checks, suit operations, emergency equipment handling, contingency drills, and cabin configuration with stowage, ensuring the crew is ready for any scenario that may arise.

In September, the full Artemis III crew and backup astronauts visited Florida together for the first time since their crew announcement earlier this year. The astronauts visited their Orion spacecraft, saw the integrated solid rocket boosters on top of the mobile launcher, and viewed the core stage undergoing final processing ahead of integration. The crew also visited commercial partners SpaceX and Blue Origin to become more oriented with the lunar lander providers’ progress, marking one more milestone in preparation for the daring Artemis III mission.

item.title: NASA says Artemis program adjustments improve shot at 2028 moon landing - CBS News
item.description:
NASA is pressing ahead with

revisions to give the agency its best shot at a lunar landing in 2028 using a lander built by either Elon Musk's SpaceX or Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, depending on which one testing indicates is the right choice, officials said Friday.

The strategy is intended to provide an alternative path to an Artemis IV landing near the moon's south pole if either company runs into supply chain problems, significant technical trouble or other issues that might trigger major delays.

To help

to that long-awaited moon landing, Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons said the agency and its contractors are working flat out to launch the Artemis III mission next year, sending four astronauts into Earth orbit to rendezvous and dock with a Blue Origin test lander and then a SpaceX Starship upper stage.

The goal is to test critical procedures close to home before launching unpiloted lunar landers on test flights leading to astronaut boots on the moon in 2028.

Artemis III to involve 3 coordinated rocket launches

The Artemis III flight will require coordinated launches of three of the world's most powerful rockets in quick succession —

, and NASA's Space Launch System. It will also require management of separate rendezvous maneuvers enabling to dock with both test landers.

The astronauts first will rendezvous and dock with Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 1 spacecraft, open hatches and float inside to test life support, communications and other critical systems.

After two days, the crew will undock and fly the Orion to the SpaceX Starship stage, docking at the top of the big rocket using a passive docking mechanism. The otherwise "off-the-shelf" Starship will not be equipped with a crew cabin and the astronauts will not be able to enter the spacecraft.

But Parsons said SpaceX already has extensive experience with life support systems, communications and navigation procedures using its Crew and Cargo Dragon spacecraft, and is making solid progress getting the Starship moon lander variant ready for flight.

Even with an off-the-shelf Starship for Artemis III, he said NASA will still gain valuable experience bringing the SpaceX and Orion spacecraft together and learning how the much smaller Orion capsule interacts with the much larger Starship.

Depending on how those flights go, NASA will have a better idea of the path forward toward the Artemis IV moon landing mission.

"We intend to wait as long as possible to make a decision about which provider is ultimately going to provide (a lander to carry) the first American astronauts back to the moon in 2028," Parsons said. "We have dedicated teams working hand in hand with both providers, marching along the way, doing everything we can to (assist)."

"Regardless of who goes first," he added, "both providers are planning for lunar landing missions in 2028."

NASA is in a self-declared space race with China, which plans to land "taikonauts" on the moon by 2030. NASA wants to get there first, to explore the lunar south pole region where ice deposits might be accessible to provide rocket fuel, air and water, and to

in the 2030s for long-duration astronaut stays.

Regardless of which lander is used for the Artemis IV mission, Parsons said NASA will launch its astronauts to space using the SLS rocket and Orion crew capsule. How the astronauts will get to the moon depends on which lander is being used.

For a SpaceX Starship landing mission, the company will launch three versions of the upper stage used with the Super Heavy booster: a propellant depot, a tanker and the lander itself. All three will use almost all of their supercold methane and liquid oxygen propellants just getting to low-Earth orbit.

For a moon mission, SpaceX will have to launch multiple tanker flights to fill up the depot's tanks. The depot, in turn, will provide the propellants needed by the lander to break out of Earth orbit and head for the moon.

When the tanker flights are almost complete, an Orion capsule, launched by an SLS rocket, will dock with the waiting Starship lander. The lander then will boost both spacecraft to the moon.

Once docked in lunar orbit, two astronauts will descend to the surface in the lander and carry out several moonwalks before blasting off to rendezvous with the Orion, which will carry the crew back to Earth.

For a Blue Origin moon landing, the company will launch three "transfer stages" using its New Glenn rocket, followed by the launch of the Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. The transfer stages will dock with the lander and boost it to orbit around the moon. An SLS rocket will launch an Orion crew capsule directly to the moon for a rendezvous and docking.

Two astronauts then will move into the lander and a transfer stage will drop it into a lower lunar orbit. The lander will descend to touchdown and, after surface operations are complete, blast off to rendezvous with the Orion, which will carry the astronauts back to Earth.

The 2028 target landing date assumes SpaceX and/or Blue Origin can demonstrate reliable, rapid-fire launches of heavy-lift rockets, large-scale in-space refueling in Earth orbit and the ability to safely land on an uncertain surface and in poor lighting.

Both companies are required to launch successful unpiloted moon landings before a flight carrying astronauts will be allowed.

For its part, SpaceX has launched 13 suborbital Super Heavy-Starship test flights since 2023 and just one, the most recent, putting a Starship into orbit. But Musk told investors earlier this week the company will be launching multiple Super Heavy-Starships per week by the end of 2027 using launch pads in Texas and Florida.

"We expect Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half next year, and then (in the) second half of next year twice weekly, or maybe even more frequently than that," he said. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said the first large-scale in-orbit refueling demonstration is planned for "early next year."

Blue Origin is still recovering from a catastrophic launch pad explosion of its New Glenn rocket in May that destroyed the booster and heavily damaged its launch pad. A new pad is being built and Blue Origin expects to resume flights late this year or in early 2027 and to send two unpiloted Blue Moon Mark 1 landers to the lunar surface by the end of next year.

Artemis IV will be "ambitious" and "extraordinarily difficult," NASA chief says

"What we are undertaking is ambitious," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "It's extraordinarily difficult, and years of decisions, both within and beyond the walls of this agency, have cost us time and resources that we never had to spare. But the agency we are reinvigorating, and the extraordinary vehicles our industry partners are building, are worth every bit of that effort. This will not be a repeat of the flags and footprints (of the Apollo program).

"These vehicles are being designed to dramatically reduce the cost of delivering mass to orbit and to the moon to support longer surface operations, enable more frequent astronaut missions, and transform what we see as a small scientific outpost into something that may one day resemble a city on the lunar surface."

He concluded his remarks by saying, "When the history books look back on this time, the politics over which rocket and landers carried us to the moon, how long it took, and at what cost will be a footnote compared to all that followed. That when the time came, the Artemis generation chose to go. And we went."

item.title: NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
As NASA returns humans to the lunar surface and establishes a long-term presence on our closest celestial neighbor, the agency and commercial human landing system providers Blue Origin and SpaceX have streamlined the designs and changed both concepts of operations for its future crewed landers.

Since NASA established initial contracts with Blue Origin and SpaceX for crewed missions to the Moon, the agency has redefined Artemis III to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between test versions of landers from each provider and the agency’s Orion spacecraft in low Earth orbit next year. In parallel, the companies are also developing crew and cargo versions of their landers for near-term Artemis missions.

“We are executing President Trump’s National Space Policy to complete the long-awaited return of American astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 and establish a Moon Base,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “We have a proven foundation in SLS and Orion, along with two lunar landers in development with Blue Origin and SpaceX. But NASA has no intention of sitting idly by as all the pieces come together. That is not how Apollo succeeded, and it is not how the near-impossible is achieved. NASA is energized, our core capabilities are being rebuilt, our machine shops are running 24/7, and our experts are in the field attacking the critical path. We are building a Super Bowl-caliber team to safely achieve these objectives and everything that comes next.”

Jared Isaacman

NASA Administrator

For the initial crewed missions to the Moon, Artemis astronauts will launch in the agency’s Orion spacecraft on top of the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During each Artemis mission, a commercial human landings system will link up with Orion before taking two crew members to the lunar surface while two remain aboard Orion. To accelerate development toward a 2028 landing, the Artemis landers and Orion will no longer rendezvous in a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon and instead meet up in an orbit that differs for each partner, informed by their systems.

Both companies are required to perform an uncrewed demonstration mission with their crewed landers prior to the near-term Artemis crewed missions to the Moon. NASA will certify lander systems prior to the crewed missions to ensure safety and mission success.

Starship lander concept of operations

SpaceX continues to plan for an in-space propellant aggregation approach to transfer super cold, or cryogenic, liquid propellant in space. The company will launch multiple versions of Starship to low Earth orbit prior to the launch of the Starship Human Landing System (HLS) from Florida. Similar to a gas station on Earth, the series of propellant “tanker” Starships in low Earth orbit will transfer propellant to the waiting “depot” Starship. The depot Starship will ultimately fuel the Starship lander for its journey to the Moon.

Under the revised operations, Starship HLS will await Orion and its crew in Earth orbit. The lander and Orion will rendezvous and dock in Earth orbit, then the Starship lander will perform a trans-lunar injection burn to send the combined lander and Orion stack to low lunar orbit. NASA is working to modify Orion to enable Starship to push it to the Moon. The lander will bring two crew members to the lunar surface for several days before delivering them back to Orion for the ride back to Earth.

Propellant aggregation in low Earth orbit allows for flexibility in the crew launch timing on SLS, while a trans-lunar injection burn performed by the Starship lander will enable direct access to low lunar orbit. This new concept of operations using low lunar orbit will significantly lower the amount of propellant Starship needs to aggregate in space while reducing the amount of time it can take for astronauts leaving the Moon’s surface in Starship to link back up with Orion. SpaceX will demonstrate the propellant aggregation approach during the uncrewed demonstration mission.

Blue Moon lander concept of operations

For its accelerated 2028 crewed lunar landing mission, Blue Origin will defer propellant transfer and use three transfer stages to send the Blue Moon Mark 2 Alpha Lander to the Moon. Based on existing Mark 1 and Mark 2 hardware, the stages operate like a multistage rocket. They launch into low Earth orbit, followed by the Mark 2 lander. Once docked, the stack departs for an elliptical polar orbit around the Moon, with each transfer stage separating as its propellant depletes. Compared with the previously planned near-rectilinear halo orbit, the elliptical polar orbit offers faster returns from the lunar surface to Orion, reduces Blue Moon lander propellant requirements, and maximizes the performance available by SLS.

This architecture provides multiple opportunities for SLS and Orion to launch the crew to elliptical polar orbit and dock with the Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. Two crew members then transfer to the lander and descend to the Moon’s South Pole. After surface operations, the lander returns to Orion, where the crew transfers for their journey back to Earth.

Blue Origin will incorporate lessons from earlier robotic Mark 1 missions supporting the agency’s Moon Base Program and demonstrate the full mission profile in an uncrewed lander transfer stage demonstration mission.

Returning American astronauts to the Moon

Ultimately, based on lander readiness, NASA will determine which company will be first selected to safely deliver astronauts to the Moon’s surface and back to lunar orbit in 2028. A second crewed landing opportunity will follow.

NASA is targeting two, approximately two-hour long lunar surface Moonwalks during initial surface missions. Astronauts will use the Moonwalks to collection lunar samples and test capabilities of the spacesuit provided by Axiom Space.

Earlier this year, NASA updated its contracts with Blue Origin and SpaceX for human landing systems and large cargo deliveries to the Moon. The updates align the agency’s human landing system requirements with acceleration efforts announced earlier this year to streamline Artemis mission architecture, expedite a lunar return, and support an increased mission cadence to the Moon.

Under the original HLS contracts, SpaceX’s Starship human landing system was assigned to the Artemis III and IV missions, while Blue Origin would use its Blue Moon Mark 2 human landing system for Artemis V. Under the contract realignments, both providers are participating in the Artemis III mission in low Earth orbit and neither lander provider has been assigned to a specific Artemis lunar landing mission.

“NASA and our lunar lander providers Blue Origin and SpaceX have been working hand in hand to ensure we can return American astronauts to the Moon by 2028,” said Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager.“While work to realign with our partners in support of architecture updates announced at Ignition Day in March has been underway since then, updating the contracts ensures NASA and its partners are on the same page with requirements and other milestones to ensure continued insight into lander development to support mission success and the safety of our Moon crews.”

Both Blue Origin and SpaceX have added development milestones to provide NASA with more insight into lander development efforts, reducing risk and enhancing astronaut safety in preparation for crewed Moon landings. SpaceX is adding two demonstrations of its crew cabin, called Cabin 1, for its Starship lander. Blue Origin is adding new human-in-the-loop testing and hardware readiness milestones to streamline training development as well as ground and flight operations.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery though its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

item.title: NASA Details Moon Lander Plans, With Artemis III Test Flight Set for Summer 2027 - Northeast Times
item.description:
NASA said Friday that it still plans to land astronauts on the Moon as soon as 2028. It presented a revised mission design at a news conference covered by Ars Technica.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the agency has the mandate, the resources and the backing of its stakeholders to carry it out.

Artemis III, a test flight with no landing, is expected to launch in summer 2027. Artemis IV, the landing mission, is still tracking toward 2028.

Artemis III Becomes a Two-Week Lander Test

Artemis III was once planned as a crewed trip to the lunar surface. Earlier this year it was reconfigured into a roughly two-week test of both commercial landers in Earth orbit, Scientific American reported.

Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander launches first on a New Glenn rocket. Three days later, NASA's Orion capsule will try to dock with it. Two days of testing navigation and communications systems follow.

On day six, SpaceX's Starship launches and Orion detaches from Blue Moon. Then comes a second docking, this time with Starship. The crew will not enter Starship, and that test will last two hours.

Isaacman said Artemis III will decide which lander flies on Artemis IV. NASA will wait as long as possible to choose. Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons said both companies are planning 2028 landings.

SpaceX Plan Drops the Lunar Orbit Docking

Under the new SpaceX design, a Starship lander is fueled in low-Earth orbit. It then docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew travels to the Moon in Orion, and two of the four astronauts move into Starship to land.

This removes a requirement to dock in a near-rectilinear halo orbit around the Moon, which SpaceX engineers had asked NASA to drop. NASA's cancellation of the Lunar Gateway station earlier this year resolved the issue, Ars Technica reported.

Nobody agrees on how many refueling flights Starship needs. A NASA safety panel put the figure at about 22 tanker launches on Thursday. SpaceX founder Elon Musk said six to eight. NASA officials declined to give a number on Friday.

Isaacman said six to eight was possible. He called it the ultimate potential end state of Starship.

Blue Origin Plan Skips Refueling Between Ships

Blue Origin's revised plan uses four New Glenn launches and no refueling from one spacecraft to another. Three transfer stages, modeled on the Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, go to low-Earth orbit first. The larger Blue Moon Mark 2 lander follows and links up with them.

The stack is then pushed toward the Moon.

The plan also allows Blue Moon to meet Orion in low-lunar orbit.

Hurdles Before Summer 2027

New Glenn has not flown since a rocket exploded in May. Parsons said Blue Origin expects to resume launches in November. NASA has no backup plan to fly Blue Moon on another rocket. He described the lander's test design as in good shape after design reviews.

Orion will sit on the pad atop its Space Launch System rocket, which no longer needs an upper stage for an Earth-orbit mission. Parsons said NASA will work to have it ready quickly after the Blue Origin launch.

SpaceX plans another Starship test flight next month, with upgraded Raptor engines. Its most recent flight reached orbit for the first time.

item.title: NASA's Artemis III will no longer land on the Moon—it's now a 2027 orbital test before the planned Artemis IV landing - Latin Times
item.description:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stood before reporters at Kennedy Space Center on the afternoon of Friday, October 23, 2026, and delivered something rarer than a headline: a credible checklist. Flanked by Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya and Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons, he reported that solid rocket booster integration is underway, a year-end tanking test is on the calendar, and the summer 2027 launch target for Artemis III remains intact. None of what he said was new policy. It was the progress report on a decision he made eight months earlier—and a reminder of how much still has to go right before any American astronaut sets foot on the Moon.

When NASA Rewrote the Mission Blueprint

The decision to convert Artemis III from a lunar landing into an Earth orbit test was made and announced on February 27, 2026, at a Kennedy Space Center press conference—Isaacman's first major programmatic move as NASA's 15th administrator. His diagnosis was direct: jumping from the Artemis II lunar flyby straight to a crewed Moon landing was, in his own words, "a bridge too far." A sharply critical report from NASA's independent Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel, released two days earlier, had already declared the original plan dangerously overloaded with untested technical firsts stacked into a single mission.

The historical model Isaacman invoked was deliberate. In March 1969, Apollo 9 put the lunar module through its paces in Earth orbit and gathered the data that allowed Apollo 11 to land on the Moon roughly four months later. The revised Artemis III is built on that same logic: de-risk the docking choreography in low orbit, then proceed to the surface with confidence.

Three Rockets, Two Landers, One Orbital Rehearsal

The mission requires three separate launch events. Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander test article launches first and enters a parking orbit where it can loiter for up to 30 days. NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) then lifts the Orion crew capsule and its four-person crew from Launch Pad 39B. Once Orion reaches its operating altitude of approximately 265 miles above Earth, it rendezvouses and docks with the Blue Moon test article. Up to two crew members are expected to enter the lander's cabin and run hands-on checkouts of its environmental control and life support systems—the first time a commercial Moon lander crew cabin will have been operated by astronauts in space. That phase runs roughly two days.

Orion then undocks and maneuvers toward a SpaceX Starship HLS pathfinder for an additional day of proximity and docking operations. Unlike with Blue Moon, crew members will not enter the Starship for this trial; SpaceX's Artemis III test article will not carry life support equipment. The total mission window runs 14 days under optimal conditions, with up to 17 days available if operations require more time. Ground teams will stress-test the entire launch sequence with a year-end tanking rehearsal—practicing propellant loading while the SLS "short stack" sits on the pad at Kennedy.

Blue Origin's New Glenn: Plan A Under Pressure

The path that carries the Blue Moon test article to orbit is not as clear as the mission architecture might suggest. On May 28, 2026, a New Glenn rocket exploded during a static fire test at Cape Canaveral, severely damaging Launch Complex 36—Blue Origin's only operational launch pad. The explosion touched off a serious internal NASA discussion about routing the Blue Moon lander onto an alternative rocket, including SpaceX's Falcon Heavy.

By October, the calculus had shifted. Blue Origin committed to rebuilding its pad rather than seeking a temporary alternative, and Isaacman confirmed that "plan A was always New Glenn," adding it was "looking a lot better today than it was weeks ago." The agency is monitoring Blue Origin's recovery closely but has not ruled out contingency options if the timeline slips further. The New Glenn explosion is, for now, the biggest single variable hanging over the 2027 launch window.

Meet the Crew Betting the Future on This Test

NASA announced the Artemis III crew on June 9, 2026, at Johnson Space Center in Houston. Commanding the mission is Randy Bresnik, a retired Marine Corps colonel and TOPGUN-trained test pilot completing his third orbital mission. Luca Parmitano, an Italian astronaut with the European Space Agency, fills the pilot's seat; he brings two International Space Station expeditions to this assignment. Frank Rubio—who holds the United States record for longest single spaceflight, 371 consecutive days on the ISS—and first-time flier Andre Douglas round out the crew as mission specialists. NASA astronaut Bob Hines will train alongside the four as the designated backup.

Their training window is tight: under the current summer 2027 target, the crew has roughly one year to master a mission that involves more simultaneous vehicle operations than any American crew has managed since the Apollo era.

Artemis IV Is the Real Moon Landing

Artemis III is the runway. Artemis IV is the takeoff. The first crewed American Moon landing since 1972 is planned for 2028 at the lunar South Pole, where permanently shadowed craters contain water ice deposits that scientists regard as a potential survival resource and a future fuel source for deep-space missions.

Isaacman has described Artemis III as a tiebreaker: whichever provider—Blue Origin or SpaceX—demonstrates greater operational capability during the 2027 orbital trial will carry the strongest case for the Artemis IV assignment. Neither company is guaranteed the slot. NASA's language specifies that Orion will dock with test versions of "one or both" landers, meaning a scenario where only one provider is ready remains on the table, though Isaacman has expressed confidence that both will participate.

The China Clock That Changes Everything

China's space agency has set an official target of landing astronauts on the Moon before 2030. Many analysts—pointing to the symbolic weight of 2029, the 80th anniversary of the People's Republic—believe that is China's realistic aim. If Artemis IV lands in 2028 as planned, the United States arrives at the lunar surface with at least a year to spare.

That margin rests entirely on Artemis III executing without major failures in summer 2027. A significant delay, a disqualifying deficiency in either lander, or an unresolved problem with New Glenn's return to flight does not simply push the timetable—it threatens to hand China the symbolic and strategic high ground on the Moon. Isaacman's restructuring is a calculated hedge: a structured orbital rehearsal that reduces the odds of a catastrophic failure on the mission that actually matters. Whether the hardware being assembled right now inside Kennedy's Vehicle Assembly Building delivers on that bet is the question the next twelve months will answer.

item.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission - Space
item.description:
TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission.

"If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife.

The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth, giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon. Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward.

"Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency. "Because we were getting so low."

The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites.

"The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained.

It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn.

"So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said.

The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon, or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled.

The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era.

Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing, the warning turned out to be a false alarm.

So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon.

"We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled.

"Everything is tracking. It's looking good."

Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph).

Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon.

The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

item.title: Artemis II crew faced cabin leak scare minutes before crucial Moon burn - Aerospace Global News
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II astronauts received a suspected cabin leak warning just 15 minutes before a critical engine firing that would send them towards the Moon, raising the possibility that their historic mission could be cut short before it had even left Earth’s vicinity.

The incident, which occurred on 2 April this year, was disclosed by Artemis II pilot Victor Glover during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife on 18 October.

The warning came as the Orion spacecraft approached the lowest point of its elongated orbit around Earth, preparing for the manoeuvre that would commit its four astronauts to a journey around the Moon.

“If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn,” Glover told the audience, according to Space.com.

The crew and mission controllers had to establish whether the warning indicated a genuine loss of cabin pressure. A real leak could have forced the astronauts to abandon their lunar journey, put on their spacesuits and prepare for an early return to Earth.

The warning was eventually determined to be false, allowing Orion to complete its engine firing and begin a journey that would carry humans further from Earth than ever before.

A warning at the worst possible moment

Artemis II had launched on 1 April aboard NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, carrying commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen.

Rather than heading directly for the Moon, Orion first entered a highly elliptical orbit around Earth. The trajectory gave the astronauts and flight controllers time to check the spacecraft’s life-support systems, communications and handling before committing to deep space.

By 2 April, Orion had travelled roughly 38,000 miles from Earth and was returning towards the planet for its planned translunar injection burn.

The manoeuvre was timed to take place near the spacecraft’s closest approach to Earth, at an altitude of about 100 miles.

At that point, Orion was travelling rapidly, making it an efficient place to fire the engine and gain the additional speed needed for the lunar journey.

Glover recalled Hansen looking through the window as Earth grew closer beneath them.

“I think we’re going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,” Hansen remarked, according to Glover’s account reported by Space.com.

The crew also had to contend with an environment containing more orbital debris and satellites as Orion descended towards its lowest altitude.

Then came the cabin leak alert.

Determining whether the warning was genuine became an immediate priority. The astronauts could not ignore a possible loss of cabin pressure, but delaying the engine firing could also mean missing the planned opportunity to head towards the Moon.

NASA flight director Judd Frieling subsequently confirmed during an April briefing that the alert had been a false alarm.

A record-breaking journey beyond the Moon

The successful burn began a mission that would take the four astronauts farther from Earth than any previous human crew, surpassing the record established by Apollo 13 in 1970.

As Aerospace Global News reported following Orion’s safe return, the spacecraft reached a maximum distance of 252,756 miles from Earth, exceeding Apollo 13’s record by more than 4,000 miles.

During the lunar flyby on 6 April, Orion passed approximately 4,067 miles above the Moon’s surface. The astronauts photographed the lunar landscape and carried out observations intended to support future exploration.

Over the nearly 10-day mission, Orion travelled more than 694,000 miles, completing life-support checks, spacecraft handling exercises and scientific investigations.

The mission also marked the first time humans had travelled beyond low Earth orbit since the Apollo programme ended in 1972.

Artemis II was not designed to land on the Moon. Its primary purpose was to demonstrate that Orion and its supporting systems could safely carry astronauts into deep space and bring them home.

A major contribution came from the European Space Agency’s European Service Module, built under ESA leadership and largely assembled by Airbus Defence and Space in Bremen. It supplied propulsion, electrical power, air, water and thermal control during the flight.

The module performed with sufficient precision that two planned trajectory correction burns were no longer needed, according to ESA officials.

Orion’s return clears the way for future missions

Artemis II concluded on 10 April when Orion splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego, completing NASA’s first crewed lunar mission in more than half a century.

The spacecraft endured temperatures of approximately 5,000°F during atmospheric re-entry, followed by a planned communications blackout lasting just over six minutes. Its parachutes then deployed successfully, bringing the crew safely to the ocean.

The cabin leak warning, now described publicly by Glover, offers a reminder of how easily the mission’s outcome might have changed.

Artemis II went on to break the record for the greatest distance travelled from Earth by humans before returning safely on 10 April.

The incident also showed why NASA had taken the precaution of checking Orion’s critical systems in Earth orbit before sending four astronauts on their journey around the Moon.

item.title: Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission - WIRED
item.description:
For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.

Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.

In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?

BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.

Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?

The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.

One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.

You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.

With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?

If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.

We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.

We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.

From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.

When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?

I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.

The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.

There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.

There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.

Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.
